summary: Emil Kowalski looks back on two years of building his animation course, animations.dev: how he stayed motivated, how he designed its packaging and platform, how he brought AI into it, and how it spread by word of mouth. The design lessons inside it are a compact easing decision flowchart (enter or exit uses ease-out, moving on screen uses ease-in-out, hover uses ease, constant motion uses linear, default ease-out), the point that a subtle scale-down on press makes an interface feel more responsive, and a set of named custom easings kept as CSS variables on :root. For a design system the main process lessons are that motion has to be felt through interactive demos rather than explained in text, that judgement about easing and duration is a human skill AI is not good at, that motion knowledge can be packaged as a SKILL.md for coding agents, and that a living product needs ongoing updates recorded in a changelog. Much of the page is testimonials and course promotion, which are not design rules.
key_ideas: Pick an easing curve by what the element is doing: entering or exiting the viewport gets ease-out, moving or morphing on screen gets ease-in-out, a hover change gets ease, constant motion gets linear, and anything else defaults to ease-out.
A subtle scale-down on press makes an interface feel more responsive.
Good motion work is mostly deciding what not to animate, and aims at great interfaces rather than great demos (shadcn's endorsement of the course).
People only understand motion by feeling the difference between good and bad themselves, so teaching and documenting motion needs interactive demos, not a wall of text.
Choosing the right easing and duration is judgement that AI is not good at; intuition and taste are the differentiator when software is abundant.
People who understand the code AI writes get more leverage from it.
Motion knowledge can be packaged as a SKILL.md file that coding agents use to build, review and improve animations.
Custom easing curves can be kept as a named set of CSS variables on :root.
Packaging (logo, hero, onboarding) creates the first impression and signals the care people can expect from the rest of the product.
Lower the barrier to practice: a built-in editor with no setup, auto-saved progress, and solutions as both video and text.
A product that keeps getting free updates, refreshed modules and a changelog stays alive instead of becoming a snapshot in time.
Teasing a project early can drain the motivation to finish it; a presale with a public deadline creates external pressure to ship.
Making something great and showing it to a few people lets word of mouth do the marketing, as happened with Sonner, Vaul and the course.

topics.summary: A subtle scale-down on press makes the interface feel more responsive; hero illustrations respond to hover and click; the logo melts over time through animated SVG paths.

topics.name: AI-assisted design
topics.summary: AI is good at code but weak at choosing easing curves and durations; people who understand the code get more leverage; motion knowledge packaged as a SKILL.md lets coding agents build, review and suggest improvements to animations.

topics.name: Design taste and judgement

topics.summary: Custom easing curves are kept as a named set of CSS custom properties on :root (--ease-breeze, --ease-silk, --ease-swift, --ease-nova, --ease-crisp, --ease-glide shown out of 18).

rules.rule: Use ease-out for any element entering or exiting the viewport.
rules.why: The course's easing decision flowchart assigns ease-out to entering and exiting elements.
rules.evidence: Easing Decision Flowchart, 'Is the element entering or exiting the viewport? Yes → ease-out'

rules.rule: Use ease-in-out for an element that moves or morphs while it stays on screen.
rules.why: The flowchart assigns ease-in-out to on-screen movement and morphing.
rules.evidence: Easing Decision Flowchart, 'Is it moving/morphing on screen? Yes → ease-in-out'

rules.rule: Use ease for hover changes.
rules.why: The flowchart assigns ease to hover changes.
rules.evidence: Easing Decision Flowchart, 'Is it a hover change? Yes → ease'

rules.rule: Use linear for constant motion; no other branch of the flowchart gives linear.
rules.why: The flowchart assigns linear to constant motion and to nothing else.
rules.evidence: Easing Decision Flowchart, 'Is it constant motion? Yes → linear'

rules.rule: When an animation is not entering or exiting, not moving or morphing on screen, not a hover change and not constant motion, default to ease-out.
rules.why: The flowchart's fallback branch is ease-out.
rules.evidence: Easing Decision Flowchart, 'Default → ease-out'

rules.rule: Choose each easing by walking the questions in order: entering or exiting the viewport, then moving or morphing on screen, then hover change, then constant motion.
rules.why: The flowchart is ordered this way, so the enter/exit check wins before the others are considered.
rules.evidence: Easing Decision Flowchart

rules.rule: Give pressable elements a subtle scale-down on press.
rules.why: It makes the interface feel more responsive.
rules.evidence: The course platform, caption under the 'Paste' demo

rules.rule: Treat motion work as mostly deciding what not to animate, and aim at great interfaces rather than great demos.
rules.why: shadcn's endorsement of the course: design engineering is mostly deciding what not to animate, and the course is about great interfaces, not great demos.
rules.evidence: shadcn testimonial, 'Somewhere along the way, design engineering became about animations and slick demos'

rules.rule: Do not accept AI-chosen easing curves and durations without review by someone with trained motion judgement [inferred].
rules.why: Choosing the right easing curves and duration is something AI is not great at, and the right judgement is key; the review step itself is not stated in the source.
rules.evidence: Animations and AI, 'how to choose the right easing curves, duration, etc. Something AI is not great at'

rules.rule: Make sure the people shipping animation code understand how the code works, even when a model wrote it.
rules.why: Those who clearly understand the code will be even more leveraged; understanding the code is still extremely valuable.
rules.evidence: Animations and AI, 'Understanding how the code works is still extremely valuable.'

rules.rule: Package the project's motion knowledge (such as the easing flowchart) as a SKILL.md file that coding agents load, so they can build, review and suggest improvements to animations.
rules.why: The skill file gives immediate value and lets agents review animations, suggest improvements, build animations and answer motion questions.
rules.evidence: Animations and AI, 'students get a SKILL.md file that they can feed to coding agents'

rules.rule: Keep custom easing curves as a named set of CSS custom properties on :root (--ease-breeze, --ease-silk and so on); not repeating raw cubic-bezier values is the likely benefit [inferred].
rules.why: This is how Emil's set of 18 custom easing functions, which he uses in his own animation work, is written; the page gives no reason for the format.
rules.evidence: Bonus features, 'A set of 18 custom easing functions that I use in my animation work.' (the numbers are exact; the extracted code block adds spaces inside cubic-bezier( ), removed here so the values are valid CSS)

rules.rule: When a component stacks a duplicate copy of its icon and label as a visual overlay (for example a 'Hold to Delete' overlay), mark the duplicate aria-hidden="true".
rules.why: The course's ClipPathButton starter hides the overlay copy; the reason is not stated, but it keeps assistive technology from reading the label twice [inferred].
rules.evidence: Code Playground, 'ClipPathButton ... aria-hidden = "true" className = "hold-overlay"' (spaces around = removed)

rules.rule: Explain every motion concept with an interactive demo people can play with, not with text alone.
rules.why: It is essential: people need to feel the difference between good and bad, and the only way is to experience it themselves, like touching a physical object to understand its texture.
rules.evidence: The course platform, 'Each lesson is packed with interactive demos.'

rules.rule: Do not present a visual subject such as animation as a dry wall of text.
rules.why: Nobody wants to read a dry wall of text when the subject is that visual; demos are also more fun.
rules.evidence: The course platform, 'Nobody wants to read a dry wall of text'

rules.rule: For technical concepts built up in steps (such as SVG path commands), use a step-through demo with Previous and Next that shows what each new step changes.
rules.why: As you press the arrow the shape is drawn progressively, showing how each new command affects the SVG.
rules.evidence: The course platform, 'The demo below is used in the SVG lesson'

rules.rule: Put a built-in code editor next to exercises so people can practise without cloning a repo or setting up a development environment.
rules.why: It lowers the barrier to working on the exercises.
rules.evidence: The course platform, 'It lowers the barrier to work on the exercises.'

rules.rule: Auto-save work in progress in editors and exercises so stopping midway loses nothing.
rules.why: If you stop in the middle of an exercise, your progress won't be lost.
rules.evidence: your code is automatically saved, so if you ever stop in the middle of an exercise

rules.rule: Offer every walkthrough both as a video and as a written version.
rules.why: Some people prefer the written version.
rules.evidence: The course platform, 'a written version for those who prefer it'

rules.rule: When teaching something as complex as animation, build a platform tailored to the topic with interactive demos, exercises and custom components.
rules.why: It makes the learning experience more engaging and effective.
rules.evidence: The course platform, 'I need a platform tailored to the topic'

rules.rule: Do not publicly tease that you are working on a project. (Emil's contrast is the presale he offered when he had zero content for the course: people had already paid and he had set a public deadline.)
rules.why: Emil calls teasing ui.land a mistake: talking about it already felt rewarding enough, so he was less motivated to finish it; it was teased in December of 2021 and launched in January 2023.
rules.evidence: A mistake I made previously with a project called ui.land was teasing that I was working on it

rules.rule: Consider committing publicly with a presale and a public deadline before building, if you can handle the pressure.
rules.why: People who have already paid create external motivation to finish.
rules.evidence: The work, 'I set a public deadline and had to stick to it'

rules.rule: Invest in the look and feel (the packaging) of a product, not only its core content.
rules.why: People love beautiful things, and the packaging creates the initial impression.
rules.evidence: The packaging, 'People love beautiful things'

rules.rule: Consider deriving the brand mark from the quality people associate with the work (for example 'buttery smooth' animation became a butter cube) and reuse it across the site in various forms.
rules.why: The butter-cube logo came from how people describe good animation and is used across the site.
rules.evidence: The packaging, 'I thought using a butter cube would be a good idea'

rules.rule: Consider small interactive details in the first things people see, such as hero illustrations that animate on hover and respond to clicks, or an easter egg that changes over time.
rules.why: Packaging creates the initial impression, and the hero also shows what the course enables people to do.
rules.evidence: The packaging, 'Hover or click on them to see different interactions.'

rules.rule: Design the first screen people see after signing up so it sets the tone and shows the care to expect from the rest of the product.
rules.why: The onboarding is part of the packaging and the first impression of the product itself; the Motion Passport welcome page sets the tone.
rules.evidence: The packaging, 'Another important aspect of the packaging is the onboarding'

rules.rule: Treat the product as a living thing: keep shipping updates, and refresh existing sections as you learn better ways to explain them.
rules.why: It keeps the product from dying out as a snapshot in time; Emil fully refreshed the theory module as he learned to teach better.
rules.evidence: Bonus features, 'not a snapshot in time, but rather a living entity that evolves'

rules.rule: Record every update on a changelog page.
rules.why: To document all the updates.
rules.evidence: Bonus features, 'To document all the updates, I created a changelog page.'

rules.rule: Go the extra mile to make things great; do not ship something mediocre.
rules.why: People naturally share things they like; Emil tries to make things he would be proud of, and says it won't always work but there is no point in making something mediocre.
rules.evidence: The marketing, 'there's no point in making something mediocre'

rules.rule: After making something great, make sure at least a few people see it and let word of mouth carry it.
rules.why: If you create great things and a few people see them, word will spread; organic marketing is the best kind.
rules.evidence: The marketing, 'If you create great things, and make sure a few people see them'

rules.rule: Aim to make a product that people cannot stop talking about.
rules.why: It is a win for everyone: users get value, the maker helps more people, and the product gets more exposure.
rules.evidence: The marketing, 'You have to create a product that people just can’t stop talking about.'

rules.rule: Ship the knowledge file for coding agents (the SKILL.md) as part of the product's ongoing updates, so existing users get it too.
rules.why: The 'Animations and AI' lesson was born from the free updates, and its skill file is free as part of them.
rules.evidence: Bonus features, 'The skill file included in that lesson is also free as part of the ongoing updates.'

rules.rule: Consider shipping a curated collection of trusted resources (articles, videos, personal websites) alongside the core material.
rules.why: The Vault collects highly curated resources that helped Emil over the years, as a bonus students can learn from.
rules.evidence: Bonus features, 'One of them is the Vault'

decisions.question: Which easing curve should this animation use?

options.name: ease-out
options.effect: The flowchart's curve for elements entering or exiting the viewport, and its default.
options.when: The element enters or exits the viewport, or no other branch applies.

options.name: ease-in-out
options.effect: The flowchart's curve for elements that move or morph while on screen.
options.when: The element is moving or morphing on screen.

options.name: ease
options.effect: The flowchart's curve for hover changes.

options.name: linear
options.effect: The flowchart's curve for constant motion.

decisions.recommendation: Pick by the element's job using the flowchart, and fall back to ease-out; this is a grouping of curves by role [inferred].

decisions.question: How should motion decisions be explained to people learning or choosing them?

options.name: Written explanation
options.effect: A wall of text; people cannot really understand motion until they experience it.
options.when: Not recommended for a visual subject like animation.

options.name: Interactive demos
options.effect: People play with the concept and feel the difference between good and bad themselves.
options.when: Every motion concept; the source calls it essential.

options.name: Step-through demo
options.effect: Previous and Next controls reveal the concept one step at a time, showing what each step changes.
options.when: Technical concepts built up in steps, such as SVG path commands.

options.name: Video plus written walkthrough
options.effect: Each exercise solution is available in the format people prefer.

decisions.recommendation: Use interactive demos throughout, step-through demos for technical build-ups, and both video and written walkthroughs for solutions, because people need to feel the difference themselves.

decisions.question: How should AI be brought into motion work?

options.name: Let AI choose easing and duration
options.effect: Fast, but AI is not great at choosing the right easing curves and duration.

options.name: Human judgement plus a motion SKILL.md for agents
options.effect: People keep the judgement; agents get the house motion knowledge to build, review and suggest improvements.
options.when: Whenever coding agents build or review animations.

decisions.recommendation: Develop intuition and understand the code, and give coding agents a SKILL.md with the motion knowledge; the right judgement is key.

decisions.question: Should the product be a finished snapshot or a living thing that keeps changing, and how are changes communicated?

options.name: Snapshot in time
options.effect: The product dies out after launch.

options.name: Living product with ongoing updates and a changelog page
options.effect: People keep learning new things; refreshed sections improve how things are explained; every update is documented.
options.when: Anything people keep using over time.

decisions.recommendation: A living product with ongoing updates, documented on a changelog page.
decisions.evidence: Bonus features, 'a living entity that evolves' and 'I created a changelog page'

decisions.question: How do you stay motivated to finish a large project?

options.name: Tease it early
options.effect: Talking about it feels rewarding enough that motivation to finish drops; ui.land took from December 2021 to January 2023.

options.name: Presale with a public deadline
options.effect: People have already paid, so there is external pressure to deliver on time.
options.when: When you can handle the pressure.

decisions.recommendation: A presale with a public deadline, as long as you can handle the pressure.

process.detail: Avoid teasing the project; instead open a presale with a public deadline so people who paid create external motivation.

Create a logo from the quality people associate with the work (buttery smooth became a butter cube), reuse it across the site, add interactive hero illustrations and small easter eggs, and design the welcome screen (Motion Passport) to set the tone.

process.step: Build a platform fit for the subject
process.detail: Pack each lesson with interactive demos people can play with, use step-through demos for technical build-ups, and add a built-in code editor that auto-saves so there is no setup.

process.step: Write exercises with solutions in two formats
process.detail: Give each exercise a video walkthrough and a written version of the solution.
Ask in order: entering or exiting the viewport (ease-out), moving or morphing on screen (ease-in-out), hover change (ease), constant motion (linear); otherwise ease-out.
Turn the motion knowledge into a SKILL.md that coding agents load to build, review and improve animations, while people keep developing their own judgement and understanding of the code.
Ship ongoing updates, refresh sections when you learn to explain them better, and record every update on a changelog page.
Go the extra mile, make sure a few people see the result, and let word of mouth spread it.

caveats: Most of the page promotes Emil's paid course (animations.dev), a waitlist with preview lessons, and a newer course (aiforui.dev); these plugs are not design rules.
Most of the text is testimonials from other people; their praise, and claims such as Delphi requiring the course, are third-party opinions.
The 'deciding what not to animate' idea comes from shadcn's testimonial, not from Emil's own text on this page.
The easing flowchart is only a snippet of a larger, multi-file skill that is part of the paid course.

Only 6 of the 18 custom easings appear in the fetched text. All six visible curves have both control points below the diagonal, which makes them ease-in shaped, so they do not fit the flowchart's ease-out branch for entering elements [inferred].
The scale-down-on-press demo gives no scale value, duration or easing in the text.
The aria-hidden overlay and trash icon come from an exercise starter file; the article does not explain them, and styles.css is not shown.
The page has no publish date; tweets are dated up to January 2026, and the note that LLMs could not help much in 2024 is time-bound.
The comment that polished animation depends on framer-motion because of springs is a reader comment, not Emil's view.
Tweet like counts and the 10,000 enrolment figure are snapshots at the time of writing.
Code values (the cubic-bezier easings and aria-hidden="true") are written in normal CSS and JSX spacing; the extracted text adds spaces inside them, but every number and name is exact.
The page states no durations and no scale value for press feedback; do not attribute duration numbers to this source.
